beats.narration_text: This week's learning focus was Infrastructure as Code with Terraform, and understanding exactly how Cloud Run's billing model works — which is what makes real cost optimization possible.

props.segment: Week 8 Technical Learnings — Terraform & Cloud Run Billing Fundamentals
props.runningText: Infrastructure as Code → Terraform core concepts → idempotency → billing → cost levers…
output: Terraform (Infrastructure as Code) + Cloud Run's billing model
what makes real cost optimization possible

beats.role_note: slide 2 -- manual setup vs. version-controlled, reviewable config
beats.narration_text: Infrastructure as Code means defining cloud resources in version-controlled configuration files instead of creating them by hand. The core benefit is that infrastructure changes become reviewable, like a code change — proposed in a pull request, reviewed before it ships, and rolled back if needed, rather than existing only as a memory of steps someone once ran manually.

nodes.d: undocumented, inconsistent — a memory of steps someone once ran
version-controlled, reviewable — proposed in a PR, rolled back if needed

props.caption: An infrastructure change becomes reviewable, like any other code change.

beats.narration_text: Terraform works through a few core concepts: providers, which represent a cloud platform like Google Cloud; resources, which are the individual things being managed, like a registry or an IAM binding; and a plan-then-apply workflow, where Terraform first shows exactly what will change before anything actually happens — removing the guesswork from infrastructure changes.

nodes.d: a cloud platform, e.g. Google Cloud
individual things managed — a registry, an IAM binding
preview — shows exactly what will change
execute — only after the plan is reviewed

props.caption: Removes the guesswork from infrastructure changes — nothing happens before it's previewed.

beats.role_note: slide 4 -- applying repeatedly converges, never duplicates
beats.narration_text: A key property of Terraform is idempotency — applying the same configuration multiple times always converges to the same result, rather than creating duplicate resources. It achieves this by maintaining a state file that records what already exists, which it compares against the configuration on every run.

nodes.d: compares state vs. config — same end result, no duplicates

props.caption: Idempotency: running it again never creates a second copy of what already exists.

beats.role_note: slide 5 -- request-based billing, not idle time
beats.narration_text: Cloud Run's default billing model charges for CPU and memory only while an instance is actively handling a request — not for idle time. Understanding this is essential, because it means the real cost levers aren't abstract — they're concrete settings: how many instances can scale to zero, how much concurrency each instance handles, and how generously memory is allocated per instance.

nodes.d: no requests being handled — no charge
CPU + memory billed for the duration

props.caption: The real cost levers are concrete settings, not abstract traffic patterns.

beats.narration_text: The practical levers are: minimum instances, which trades cost for eliminating cold starts; maximum instances, which caps runaway scaling cost; concurrency, which determines how many requests one instance serves at once; and right-sizing CPU and memory so you're not paying for capacity the application never uses.

nodes.d: trades cost for eliminating cold starts
requests served per instance, at once
don't pay for capacity never used

props.caption: Four concrete settings — not abstractions — are what actually control the bill.

beats.role_note: slide 7 -- the closing line, Claude cream skin
beats.narration_text: Put together, Terraform and Cloud Run's billing model connect because when infrastructure is defined as code, cost settings become explicit, reviewable decisions — not defaults left unexamined.

props.artifactHeading: You optimize what you can measure — and what you can measure, you can define in code.
artifactLines: Infrastructure as Code: cloud resources defined in version-controlled, reviewable configuration.
Terraform: provider → resources → plan (preview) → apply (execute) — no guesswork.
Idempotency: a state file means re-applying the same config never duplicates resources.
Cloud Run bills by request, not idle time — min/max instances, concurrency, and sizing are the real levers.
When infrastructure is code, cost settings become explicit decisions, not unexamined defaults.
